samples.summary: Revocation reconcile cannot see archive-only documents, so content from a workspace the user was removed from is never erased
samples.evidence:
`purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` builds its candidate list with `store.storedDocumentIds()` (offline-erase.ts:351), and that method enumerates only the `headers` object store (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:930-942, `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, ...)`). But `remove()` deletes the header and writes the content into the separate `archives` store — so a document that hit `LocalChangesDropped` has an archive and NO header. It is therefore absent from `storedDocumentIds()`, `purgeDocument(id, {archives:'drop'})` is never called for it, and the archive survives the reconcile.

This is the exact case the design says the reconcile exists for. `workspaces.ts` removeMember documents that the removed member's own device "is reached by nothing that happens here, so it reconciles on its own: OfflineRuntime asks the server what it may still read on every session and drops what is no longer listed (purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments)". For an archived document that promise is not kept.

Chain: user A opens sheet-X in workspace W; the SDK hits one of the three LocalChangesDropped paths, so the full compressed document moves to `archives`. An owner removes A from W. On A's next session purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments sees no header for sheet-X and drops nothing. OfflineRuntime's recovery toast then offers the archive back and recoverOfflineCopy creates `sheet-X (offline copy)` — a permanent, server-side document A owns, containing content from a workspace A was removed from.

The existing test misses it because it re-seeds the live entry after archiving: offline-erase.test.ts "drops what the server no longer lists, archives included" calls store.remove(...) and then `await seed(store, "pk/wb:1:sheet-gone/sheet-gone")` again, restoring the header the real scenario would not have. The archive-only shape is untested.

Contrast showing the fix exists: deleteWorkspace/removeMember pass ids from the server listing, so purgeDocument reaches dropArchivesForDocument (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:945) regardless of headers. Only the reconcile derives its ids from local headers.

samples.summary: Offline-copy recovery re-materializes archived content with no authorization check; a 403 from the server is swallowed and treated as a missing title
samples.evidence:
`offerRecoverableWork` fetches the document only to decorate the toast, and swallows every error: `try { title = (await fetchDocument(described.id)).title || title } catch { /* Keep the fallback */ }` (offline-runtime.tsx:204-209). fetchWithAuth + assertOk throw on a 403 exactly as on a 404, so the code cannot distinguish "deleted upstream" (the justification in the comment) from "you are no longer permitted to read this". Either way it renders the `Save a copy` action, and recoverOfflineCopy (offline-copy-recovery.ts) then calls createDocument(...) + applyImportedContent(...) with the archived content — no re-check of access anywhere on the path.

So the only thing between a revoked user and re-materializing the content is that the archive should already have been purged — which finding #1 shows it is not. Together: archive survives revocation -> recovery offers it -> the 403 that would have refused it is discarded -> content is written back to the server as a new document the user owns.

Even independently of finding #1 this is a missing gate: a server response that explicitly denies access is the strongest signal available here, and it is the one signal the code throws away. Treating a 403 (as distinct from a 404) as "leave this archived, do not offer it" would close the hole at this layer.

samples.summary: isOpenInAnyTab fails open as "open" for the erasure callers, silently disabling both the revocation purge and the 30-day sweep on browsers with LockManager.request but no query
samples.evidence:
isOpenInAnyTab returns `true` — meaning "assume open, do not delete" — both when supportsDurableSession() is false (durable-session.ts:211-213) and when navigator.locks.query() throws (durable-session.ts:228-230). That default is correct for its original caller, eviction, where refusing to delete costs a failed write. It is inverted for the two erasure callers, where refusing to delete costs retained content the user is no longer entitled to.

Reachability is not hypothetical, because the capability probe and the call disagree about which API they need. supportsDurableSession() checks only `typeof navigator.locks.request === "function"` (durable-session.ts:57-65); it never probes `query`. On a runtime shipping LockManager.request but not LockManager.query, durability is ENABLED — entries and archives get written — while line 215 throws TypeError on every call and the catch answers `true` forever.

Consequences, both permanent on such a runtime:
- purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments passes `skipOpen: true` and `isOpenElsewhere: isOpenInAnyTab` (offline-erase.ts:356, offline-runtime.tsx), so purgeDocument's `if (options.skipOpen && (await this.isLive(key))) continue;` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:886) skips EVERY entry. Access revoked by someone else is never cleaned up.
- collectStale's isLive check skips every live entry for the same reason, so the 30-day backstop the design's cleanup table names as the catch-all for every other row never collects anything.

A transient query() rejection costs one sweep; the missing-query case costs all of them. Fix is to fail in the safe direction per caller — erasure should treat "cannot tell" as "not open" — or require `query` in supportsDurableSession() so durability is refused where the guard cannot work.

samples.summary: An expired session leaves full document content (archives) plus the identity marker on a possibly shared device, with no retry ever scheduled
samples.evidence:
fetchWithAuth's 401 arm calls `logout({ eraseLocalData: "keep-archives" })` (auth.ts:252-265), and eraseOfflineDataOnLogout({keepArchives:true}) takes the branch calling only `forgetPendingErase(who)` — it deliberately does NOT call rememberOfflineUser(undefined) and records no pending erase. After an involuntary sign-out the device still holds (a) every archive for that account, each a whole compressed document, and (b) localStorage['wafflebase-offline-user'] naming them.

Nothing schedules a retry: no pending-erase marker is written, so retryPendingOfflineErase() does nothing next session. The only thing that ever removes those archives is collectStale at 30 days, run by whoever next signs in on that browser.

The design argues the trade explicitly (an expired cookie is not a decision; archives are the only copy of unreconciled work), and the content is not readable through the app by a different account — listArchives/loadArchive are userId-scoped. So this is on-disk retention rather than in-app disclosure, reported as documented-but-real residue rather than as a flaw in the reasoning. Worth noting a session expiring is, by the design's own words, "the commonest way one ends on a shared machine" — the population the per-device opt-in was built for.

samples.summary: deleteWorkspace silently purges nothing when the pre-delete workspace lookup fails and the route param is a slug
samples.evidence:
documentIdsIn(ref) resolves the reference with `await fetchWorkspace(ref).catch(() => undefined)` and filters on `document.workspaceId === ref || (!!workspace && document.workspaceId === workspace.id)`. Every caller takes `ref` straight from the /w/:workspaceId/... route param, which the app navigates with the SLUG, while document.workspaceId is always the id. If the lookup fails for any reason — transient 5xx, network blip, workspace already gone — neither disjunct matches, `doomed` is [], and purgeOfflineDocuments([], {dropArchives:true}) returns immediately at its `documentIds.length === 0` guard.

Local copies and archives of every document in a deleted workspace then stay on the requester's disk while the code and its tests read as though the purge ran. The "still deletes when the listing fails" test asserts exactly `purge` called with [], pinning the resilience but not the cleanup.

Lower severity because this is the requester's own device and their own content, and purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments would eventually cover it — except that, per finding #1, that backstop misses archive-only entries, so the two gaps compound for a workspace whose documents were archived.

samples.summary: Lock names expose other signed-in accounts' user ids and open document keys to any script in the origin
samples.evidence:
Elections are taken under `wb-durable:{userId}:{docKey}` (durableLockName, durable-session.ts), and navigator.locks.query() at line 215 returns held lock names for the whole origin, not just the caller's tab. Any script running in the origin — including the app under a different signed-in account in another tab — can enumerate which user ids are currently editing which document keys on this machine.

Impact is limited: same-origin, same browser profile, and an attacker who can run script in the origin has more direct routes to the same data. But the lock name is the one place in this design where a user identifier is written somewhere with no scoping at all, and it need not be — a per-origin salted hash of `{userId}:{docKey}` would elect exactly as well while revealing nothing, since the name is never parsed, only prefix- and suffix-matched at durable-session.ts:222-227.

verdict.reason: Verified in full. purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments (offline-erase.ts:351) builds its candidate id list from store.storedDocumentIds(), which enumerates only the headers store via headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, ...) (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:930-942) and never touches ARCHIVES. remove() writes an ArchiveRecord into ARCHIVES (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:802) and then unconditionally deletes the header (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:810), so a document that hit a LocalChangesDropped path exists as an archive with no header. Such an id is absent from the candidate list, so purgeDocument(id, {archives:"drop"}) is never invoked for it and dropArchivesForDocument (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:945), reachable only from purgeDocument (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:902-904), never runs. No downstream guard compensates: listArchives filters on userId only (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:972-983), listRecoverableWork/rehydrateArchive perform no access check (offline-copy.ts:148), and offline-runtime.tsx:181-221 offers the archive back via recoverOfflineCopy, creating a new server-side document owned by the removed user containing workspace content they may no longer read. The cited test genuinely re-seeds the live entry after archiving (offline-erase.test.ts:388-389), so the archive-only shape is untested. Contrast confirmed: the delete/removeMember callers pass server-supplied ids (offline-erase.ts:288-292) and so do reach the archive drop. This is retention of data past revoked read authority plus re-materialization into an owned document — an access-control weakness in the security lane, and it breaks the guarantee documented at workspaces.ts:151.

verdict.reason: The quoted code is present verbatim (offline-runtime.tsx:204-209 swallows every fetchDocument error, and api/documents.ts:46-56 confirms assertOk throws identically on 403 and 404), so the presence claim is factually accurate. It is not blocking under the security lens for three independently sufficient reasons. (1) No authorization boundary is crossed: recovery writes via createDocument, and both backend create endpoints enforce workspaceService.assertMember(workspaceId, userId) at document.controller.ts:124 and :203, so a revoked user cannot write content back into the workspace they lost. applyImportedContent(created.id, content) at offline-copy-recovery.ts:211 writes only into the freshly created, user-owned document returned at :210 — never into the original revoked document. (2) No cross-user exposure: listArchives filters by the BY_USER index on this.userId (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:976) and loadArchive independently re-checks row.userId !== this.userId returning undefined (:1000), so the path can only surface archives written by the same signed-in user on the same device. (3) The requested gate is client-side over data already sitting in plaintext in the attacker's own IndexedDB, written by their own session; a revoked user reads it from devtools regardless, so suppressing the toast denies them nothing. The 403 path also discloses nothing, since the title is only used on success and otherwise falls back to 'Untitled'. The finding itself concedes the only real control is purging the archive ("which finding #1 shows it is not"), making this derivative of that separate retention finding rather than an independent gate; the enforceable control is purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments (offline-runtime.tsx:130 -> offline-erase.ts:329-361, which does pass archives: "drop"). At most a minor hardening suggestion, not a blocking major. No secret exposure, injection, crypto, IDOR, SSRF, or traversal issue on this path.

Both erasure callers consume that value unnormalized: purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments passes isOpenElsewhere (offline-erase.ts:347) with skipOpen: true (356-360), and purgeDocument skips every entry at wafflebase-doc-store.ts:886 via isLive (397-402); collectStale skips every entry at wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1118. offline-runtime.tsx:64-71, 101, 130-133 wires both to isOpenInAnyTab in production and constructs the store unconditionally, so previously-stored entries are reachable even where durability is disabled. finding.summary: Another account's archived document content is never collected by any sweep, so an expired session leaves full documents on a shared device indefinitely
finding.evidence:
`collectStale` sweeps live entries across all users (deliberately, per the comment at line 1005: "a shared device's other account is precisely the one that never comes back to run its own housekeeping"), but the archive sweep at line 1037 passes `this.userId` as `onlyUser`, so `dropArchivesWhere` skips every archive row belonging to anyone else. Cross-checking every other caller of `dropArchivesWhere`: `dropAllForUser` (line 985) uses `IDBKeyRange.only(userId)` and is only ever invoked with the signed-in or the pending-erase identity, and `dropArchivesForDocument` filters on `BY_USER` = `this.userId`. There is no path that collects a departed account's archives.

The attack/exposure chain: user A opts in on a shared machine and edits. Their session cookie expires — which `api/auth.ts:255-266` itself calls "the commonest way a session ends" — so `fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm calls `logout({ eraseLocalData: 'keep-archives' })`, and `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` (offline-erase.ts:165-169) deliberately spares the archives AND, on that branch, does not clear `rememberOfflineUser`. A never returns to that machine. Their archives — whole gzip'd CRDT snapshots plus change logs, i.e. document text — now sit in the origin's IndexedDB forever: user B's session sweeps A's *live* entries at 30 days but provably cannot touch A's archives, A's own sweep never runs, and `dropAllForUser` is never called with A's id again. Anyone with the browser profile (the next user of the shared workstation, devtools, forensic imaging) reads them directly.

This is the exact population the design's own § Storage cleanup table names the 30-day sweep as the backstop for, with archives carved out of it and no replacement backstop supplied.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual claim is not true of this repository. It asserts the archive sweep in `collectStale` passes `this.userId` as `onlyUser`, causing `dropArchivesWhere` to skip other accounts' archives. In the working tree, wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1129 calls `this.dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range)` with exactly two arguments — no `onlyUser`. In `dropArchivesWhere` (1242-1266), `theirs` is `undefined` when `onlyUser === undefined` (1253-1260), so the skip guard `if (theirs && !theirs.has(id)) continue;` (1263) never fires and every archive row under the `archivedAt` cutoff is deleted regardless of owner. The file's own comments (1101-1110, 1126-1128) state this policy explicitly: archives are swept "across every account on this device," with identity scoping deliberately retained only for reading/spending another's archives (`listArchives` at 976, the `row.userId !== this.userId` gate at 1000). I enumerated the other callers: `dropAllForUser` (1072) is `BY_USER`-scoped by design so signing out of one account does not destroy another's work, and `dropArchivesForDocument` (945-950) is user-scoped. So a departed user A's archives ARE collected by any other account's 30-day sweep via BY_ARCHIVED_AT — precisely the backstop the finding claims is absent. The claimed indefinite-retention exposure chain therefore does not exist; it rests on an argument that is not in the code. (The `onlyUser` parameter is presently unused dead code, a maintainability nit, not a security defect.)
